papers.title: A Sharp Additive Bound for the Threshold Rule in Repeated Rent-or-Buy
papers.abstract: Motivated by context management in LLM agents, we study a repeated rent-or-buy model with schedule-independent history growth and a fixed reset price $K$, a discrete form of dynamic TCP acknowledgment: every call pays as rent the history accumulated since the last reset, and a reset clears it. The classical threshold rule is $2$-competitive, and no deterministic rule guarantees a smaller ratio. We show that, measured additively, its loss is governed by the changes in the growth: if the growth is constant on $P$ runs, the threshold rule, knowing neither the runs nor the horizon, pays at most $(2P-1)K$ more than the optimal schedule chosen with hindsight, and the coefficient $2P-1$ is sharp. If the growth is only within a factor $1+\varepsilon$ of $P$ runs, the bound holds up to a factor $1+\varepsilon$ and an extra $\varepsilon K$. The proof is a potential argument built from the relative value functions of the single-rate problems. On two runs no deterministic rule guarantees a loss below $2K$. A rule that also resets when the growth decreases guarantees $2K$, while the threshold rule can lose arbitrarily close to $3K$.

papers.title: An Integrality-Gap Lower Bound of 1.2325 for Minimum Multiway Cut
papers.abstract: We prove that the integrality gap of the C\u{a}linescu-Karloff-Rabani relaxation for Minimum Multiway Cut is at least $1.2325$ when the number of terminals is large. By a result of Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz (2008), it is therefore NP-hard, under the Unique Games Conjecture, to approximate Minimum Multiway Cut within a factor of $1.2325$. This improves the previously best known lower bound of $1.20016$ due to B\'erczi, Chandrasekaran, Kir\'aly, and Madan (2020).

papers.title: Polynomial Lower Bounds for Steiner Shortcuts via Test Functions
papers.abstract: The Steiner shortcut problem asks whether every directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges admits an augmentation $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+o(1)}$ edges such that $G_+$ has the same reachability structure as $G$ (i.e. for all $s,t\in V$, $s$ reaches $t$ in $G$ iff $s$ reaches $t$ in $G_+$), and the diameter of $G_{+}$ is $m^{o(1)}$. This is a core combinatorial question underlying many reachability algorithms in the dynamic, streaming, and CONGEST models, and all parallel algorithms with almost-linear work and sublinear depth. A sequence of works ruled out such a shortcut $G_{+}$ in the non-Steiner setting where $V_{+}=\emptyset$. However, as recently shown by Bernstein et al. [STOC '26], all known non-Steiner lower-bound constructions fail once Steiner vertices $V_{+}$ are allowed. This paper rules out almost-optimal Steiner shortcuts: we show an infinite family of graphs $G=(V,E)$ with the property that, for any $\varepsilon>0$, a Steiner shortcut $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+\varepsilon}$ edges must have diameter at least $n^{1/56-O(\varepsilon)}$. Our construction strengthens the standard non-Steiner lower-bound framework via an additional structure that allows Steiner vertices to be replaced by original vertices; we can then reduce back to the standard arguments without Steiner vertices. This new structure is achieved via a new general strategy based on test functions, which is quite flexible and can potentially be extended to applications beyond our work. We also generalize our lower bound to exact Steiner hopsets in undirected graphs and to depth reduction for monotone circuits. The latter significantly strengthens the classical lower bound based on Sylvester matrices.

papers.title: $L_1$ versus $L_2$ Clustering: When Does the Choice of Norm Matter?
papers.abstract: We study how well approximation guarantees for clustering under one norm translate into guarantees under another. Specifically, we compare $k$-clustering in $\mathbb{R}^d$ under the $L_1$ and $L_2$ objectives, defined as the sums of Manhattan and Euclidean distances, respectively. In the worst case, the elementary relationship between these norms yields a $\sqrt{d}$ approximation bound, which is already tight for $k=2$. We therefore investigate whether stronger guarantees are possible in a natural average-case model, where the dataset is arbitrary but the coordinate system is chosen uniformly at random among all orthonormal bases. Our main result shows that, when $d=\Omega(\log k)$, with high probability over the random rotation, any $\beta$-approximate $L_1$ clustering, with optimally chosen centers for its clusters, is also an $O(\beta)$-approximation under the $L_2$ objective. We also establish an expected approximation ratio of $O(\beta\min\{\sqrt{d},k^{2/d}\})$, yielding a dimension-independent bound of $O(\beta\sqrt{\log k/\log\log k})$. We obtain analogous guarantees in the reverse direction, from $L_2$ to $L_1$. We complement these results with lower bounds of $\Omega(\min\{\sqrt{d},k^{1/d}\})$ in both directions, showing that our dimension-independent guarantees have asymptotically optimal dependence on $k$ for constant $\beta$. Our proofs overcome the dependence of the algorithm's output on the random rotation using geometric projection arguments and small Euclidean coresets. In particular, our results provide guarantees for existing clustering algorithms without requiring their redesign.

papers.title: Quadratic-Time Barriers from Self-Referential SAT
papers.abstract: Under the self-referential $K$-SAT exhaustive-search hypothesis (SRK-ESH), no uniform deterministic algorithm computes exact longest common subsequence or standard edit distance on binary strings in $O(n^{2-\eta})$ time for any fixed $\eta>0$, where $n$ is the longer sequence length. The same exclusion holds for one-dimensional dynamic time warping on $\{0,1,2,4,8\}$ with absolute-difference cost and for five-symbol dynamic time warping with the discrete metric. We derive Orthogonal Vectors hardness in polylogarithmic dimension by splitting the variables of the logarithmic-width source formula into two halves. Existing sequence reductions have polynomial overhead in the dimension. Their output lengths and construction times allow a fixed saving in the target exponent to yield a fixed proportional saving in the source exponent.

papers.title: Exact $\ell_p$-CVP via Euclidean SVP in Polynomial Space
papers.abstract: We give a randomized, rank-preserving reduction from exact $\ell_p$-CVP to exact Euclidean SVP for every integer $p\ge2$. For rational inputs of bit length $\ell$ on full-rank lattices $L\subset\mathbb R^N$, the reduction uses $(Cp)^N\poly(p,\ell)$ oracle calls and additional bit operations, where $C$ is an absolute constant. It uses $\poly(p,\ell)$ working space outside the oracle, and all oracle queries have rank $N$ and $\poly(p,\ell)$ bit complexity. For $p=2$, the reduction transfers polynomial-space exact SVP algorithms to exact CVP with $2^{O(N)}\poly(\ell)$ time overhead. Instantiating it with the SVP algorithms of Kannan and of Feng, Gao and Liu yields randomized polynomial-space CVP algorithms running in time $N^{N/(2e)+o(N)}$ and $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$, respectively. For every fixed integer $p\ge3$, the same reduction yields exact $\ell_p$-CVP algorithms for arbitrary rational targets either in randomized time and space $2^{O(N)}$, or in randomized time $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$ and polynomial space. These algorithmic bounds are up to polynomial factors in $\ell$. The reduction performs local search sequentially over the cosets of \(2L\), where \(L\) is the input lattice, while tracking the excess of the current objective value over the optimum. Within a coset containing a closest vector, midpoint inequalities bound the unknown correction in terms of this excess, which in turn allows us to construct many short corrections that reduce the excess bound by a factor of four. A counting argument shows that these improving corrections form a sufficiently large fraction of the lattice points in a known search region, and a sparsification-based sampler assigns sufficiently large probability to every nonzero vector in that region, using at most one SVP call per sample. For \(p\ge3\), the same framework is extended using a diagonal weighted norm computed from the current point.

papers.title: GreedTok is a Constant-Factor Approximation for Partition-Cover Tokenization
papers.abstract: GreedTok (Lim, Tan, Choo and Lauw, NeurIPS 2025) builds a tokenizer vocabulary greedily for the partition-cover objective: choose $k$ tokens so as to maximize the number of adjacent character pairs merged when the corpus is segmented optimally. The objective is neither submodular nor supermodular, so the classical $1-1/e$ analysis does not apply, and a worst-case guarantee was left open. We prove that GreedTok is a constant-factor approximation: on every corpus and for every budget $k$ it achieves at least $0.2752$ of the optimum, and it is optimal for $k=1$. The bound holds for both the exact greedy loop and the lazy priority-queue loop of the published algorithm and its code. The key ingredient is a shift lemma: if two occurrences of a not-yet-chosen token overlap and both are still usable, they offer exactly the same gain, so GreedTok's left-to-right scoring loses nothing when occurrences collide. A per-occurrence charging argument, with window distributions certified in exact arithmetic or given in closed form, completes the proof. In the other direction, we construct corpora on which GreedTok, with adversarial tie-breaking, achieves at most a fraction of the optimum tending to $(7-\ln 2)/12\approx0.5256$ (below $0.5380$ when every greedy choice is unique). Finally, we show that the objective is NP-hard to approximate within $1-1/31580$, to our knowledge the first inapproximability result for it.

papers.title: Constant-Factor Approximations for the Biased Traveling Salesman Problem and Its Path Variant
papers.abstract: The metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a fundamental problem in combinatorial optimization that asks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle in a complete undirected graph with $N$ vertices, where edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality. The biased TSP (BTSP) is a natural generalization of the metric TSP, in which the vertex set is partitioned into $k$ subsets: edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality within each subset, while edges crossing the subsets may violate the triangle inequality by a certain bias factor. This model captures scenarios in which distances are metric only locally but may be distorted across different regions or types of vertices. In this paper, we study approximation algorithms for the BTSP and its path variant, the biased traveling salesman path problem (BTSPP), which asks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian path. Previously, constant-factor approximation algorithms were known only for the case $k=2$. Whether the BTSP and the BTSPP admit constant-factor approximation algorithms for any fixed integer $k>2$ has remained an open question. We resolve this question affirmatively. We show that both the BTSP and the BTSPP admit $O(k)$-approximation algorithms with running time $N^{O(2^k k!)}$. Moreover, for the BTSPP with $k=2$, we propose an improved $(\alpha+2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm, where $\alpha<3/2-10^{-34}$ is the best-known approximation ratio for the metric TSP, improving upon the previous ratio of $4$

papers.title: Constant-Factor Approximation Algorithms for Weighted Budgeted Multisensor Sweep Coverage
papers.abstract: Sweep coverage requires each point of interest (PoI) to be revisited by some mobile sensor at least once during every sweep period, and it underlies persistent patrolling, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure inspection. Given a set of $N$ PoIs, each associated with a nonnegative weight representing its importance, the weighted budgeted sweep coverage problem (WB-SCP) seeks routing trajectories for a budget of $M\leq N$ identical mobile sensors with a common maximum speed to maximize the total weight of the sweep-covered PoIs. For the unweighted special case in which every PoI has unit weight, the first constant-factor approximation algorithm achieves a ratio of $0.0116-O(\varepsilon)$ for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, and whether the WB-SCP itself admits such an algorithm has remained open. In this paper, we resolve this open question by proposing two constant-factor approximation algorithms for the WB-SCP. The first converts any bifactor $(\alpha,\beta)$-approximation algorithm into a $\beta/(2\alpha)$-approximation algorithm, yielding a ratio of $1/16=0.0625$. The second builds on a greedy maximum-coverage framework and improves the ratio to $1-e^{-1/2}-\varepsilon$ for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. Both algorithms also improve the best-known ratio for the unweighted case, and the second extends to heterogeneous sensors with different speeds while preserving the same guarantee.

papers.title: A Simple Discrete Newton Method for the Quickest Transshipment Problem
papers.abstract: The quickest transshipment problem is a problem defined in a dynamic network with multiple sources and multiple sinks. The goal of this problem is to send all the supplies from sources to sinks as quickly as possible. It is known that this problem can be solved in polynomial time. In particular, Schl\"oter, Skutella, and Tran proposed a strongly polynomial-time discrete Newton method for this problem. In this paper, we propose a simple polynomial-time discrete Newton method for the quickest transshipment problem.

papers.title: Sharp Limits of Graph-Based Nearest Neighbor Search on the Sphere
papers.abstract: We study the degree needed for greedy graph search to find the exact nearest neighbor from every starting point on graphs of $n$ independent data points on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^d$. For uniform data, we determine an explicit sublinear degree threshold when $d$ is proportional to $\log n$, and the threshold $2^{d/2+o(d)}$ in the dense regime $\sqrt{\log n}\ll d\ll\log n$. Above these thresholds by fixed exponent gaps, the nearest-neighbor graph succeeds from every entry for most uniform queries with high probability, with evaluation cost on the same exponential scale as its degree. Matching lower bounds hold for every graph designed after observing the sample. For nonuniform data in the dense regime, local density variation shifts the critical degree. Under explicit local regularity conditions and within a specified range of density variation, we derive a sharp worst-case degree curve and show that the nearest-neighbor graph attains it. We construct sampling densities and query distributions for which, with high probability, every graph whose degree lies below this curve by a fixed exponent gap has failing entries for most queries. Allowing fresh uniform random entries reduces the cost of exact recovery. For uniform data in the dense regime, we determine the exact exponent for the number of distinct distance evaluations over a range of degrees below the critical threshold. Independent restarts on a single graph joining points within a prescribed radius attain this exponent with high probability. Matching lower bounds hold for adaptive local exploration on threshold and nearest-neighbor graphs using entries independent of the data. Optimizing within this degree range lowers the exponent from $\frac12\log2\approx0.347$ for success from every entry to approximately $0.243$.

papers.title: Approximate Hamming Convolution via Rectangular Matrix Multiplication
papers.abstract: We study $(1 \pm \epsilon)$-approximate text-to-pattern Hamming distance: given a length-$N$ pattern and a length-$2N$ text, compute the Hamming distance at every alignment to relative error $\epsilon$. For every fixed $a \ge 0$ and $\epsilon = N^{-a}$, we give a randomized algorithm with simultaneous high-probability correctness on a logarithmic-word RAM and expected running time $\widetilde{O}(N^{\omega(4a)/2})$, where $\widetilde{O}$ suppresses subpolynomial factors and $\omega(k)$ is the exponent for multiplying an $n \times n^k$ matrix by an $n^k \times n$ matrix. With a recent rectangular bound, this improves the published bounds [CGK+20, FKN26] for $1/12 < a < (3 + \sqrt{3})/16$. In particular, the algorithm runs in expected time $\widetilde{O}(N)$ for $0 \le a \le 1/8$, extending the previous near-linear guarantee through $a = 1/12$.

papers.title: Adversarially Robust Streaming Algorithms for $(k, z)$-Clustering
papers.abstract: We design adversarially robust algorithms for dynamic geometric streams that $(1 + \epsilon)$-approximate $k$-Median and $k$-Means in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, using $\tilde{O}(kd \mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1}))$ space. This result significantly improves a recent $O(d\log n)$-approximation for $k$-Median [Gribelyuk, Lin, Woodruff, Yu, and Zhou, FOCS 2026], and is furthermore the first algorithm whose space is linear in $kd$, even in the oblivious (non-adaptive) setting. We develop several new techniques which may be of independent interest, including a new data-oblivious Euclidean primitive called hierarchical Lipschitz assignment, a robust dimensionality reduction for clustering, and a robust streaming algorithm for inner-product queries.

papers.title: Quasi-polynomial-sized vertex multicut-mimicking networks and kernelization for Vertex Multiway Cut
papers.abstract: We give deterministic polynomial-time constructions of vertex multicut-mimicking networks of quasi-polynomial size. Given a graph G, a terminal set T, and a positive integer c, our algorithm constructs a graph with |T|^7 c^{O( log c ) } vertices that preserves every minimum vertex multiway cut value of at most c, for every partition of the terminals. Setting c=|T| gives an exact vertex multicut-mimicking network with |T|^{O( log |T| ) } vertices, resolving an open question of Wahlstr\"om [ACM Transactions on Algorithms 2022], who showed a bound of \kappa^{O( log^3 \kappa)} for the edge multicut-mimicking variant, where \kappa:= \sum_{t \in T} |N_G(t)| is the capacity of the terminal set, which was later improved to \kappa^{O( log^2 \kappa)} by Anand, Lee, Li and Saranurak [STOC 2024]. As applications of our vertex multicut-mimicking network, we obtain deterministic kernels of size k^{O( log k )} for Vertex Multiway Cut, p^{O(1)} k^{O(log k)} for Vertex Multicut with p requests and |\Gamma|^{O(1)} k^{O( log k)} for Group Feedback Vertex Set, where k is the deletion budget and \Gamma is a finite group. Our first kernelization result, in particular, resolves an open question by Wahlstr\"om [ACM Transactions on Algorithms 2022], which was reiterated in a recent survey on kernelization by Jansen [Computer Science Reviews 2026]. Also, to the best of our knowledge, our kernel for Vertex Multicut is the first one whose size is completely polynomial in p and (quasi-polynomial) super-polynomial only in k. Finally, again using our vertex multicut-mimicking network for graphs, we obtain a hyperedge multicut-mimicking network for hypergraphs, which preserves hypergraph edge-multicuts of size up to c, of size |T|^{O(1)} c^{O(log c)}. Our result removes the dependence on the rank of the hypergraph from the exponent of the size bound, that existed in prior work.

papers.title: Tight Worst-Case Completion-Time Bounds for Dominant Resource Fairness
papers.abstract: Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) is an influential policy for sharing multiple resources among jobs with heterogeneous demands. It combines sharing incentive, strategy-proofness, envy-freeness, and Pareto efficiency, making it particularly attractive for shared computing systems. DRF has been implemented in major resource-management frameworks, including Apache Mesos and Hadoop YARN. DRF is also nonclairvoyant: it requires no advance knowledge of job sizes, making it practical when processing requirements are difficult to predict. This motivates understanding its completion-time performance relative to an optimal schedule that knows all job sizes. However, elementary arguments can only give an $\Omega(\sqrt D)$ lower bound and an $O(D)$ upper bound for total completion time, where $D$ is the number of resource types. In this paper, we close this gap by proving that DRF is $\Theta(\sqrt D)$-competitive. More generally, for every fixed real $q\geq1$, we show that DRF is $\Theta(D^{1/(q+1)})$-competitive for the $\ell_q$ norm of completion times, with larger $q$ placing greater emphasis on late-finishing jobs. These bounds hold with arbitrary release times. We also give a refined analysis of total completion time for small $D$.

papers.title: Solving Linear Programs in the Matrix Multiplication Time
papers.abstract: We give a randomized algorithm for feasible bounded-box linear programs with $n$ variables and $d\le n=O(d)$ linearly independent equality constraints. For additive accuracy $\epsilon$, its expected running time is $O((n^\omega+n^2\log n)\log(1/\epsilon))$, where $\omega$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. This answers the matrix-multiplication-time open question posted in Song's Ph.D. thesis [Son19] in this setting.

papers.title: Sum-of-Squares Refutation Implies Planted Recovery for Semirandom CSPs
papers.abstract: We give a $n^{O(\ell)}$-time algorithm for solving semirandom planted instances of a $k$-ary Boolean constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) with $m \gtrsim \left(\frac{n}{\ell}\right)^{k/2} \ell \, \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ constraints, for any choice of the runtime parameter $\ell$. Up to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factors, this matches the known runtime vs.\ number of constraints trade-off for refuting semirandom CSPs, as well as the trade-off for solving fully random planted CSPs. Prior work on designing algorithms for semirandom CSPs follows a high-level blueprint of decomposing the constraint hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ of the instance into pieces, each with an explicit pseudorandom property that allows the standard algorithm for random CSPs to succeed on every piece. We depart considerably from this framework and instead implicitly \emph{learn} such a decomposition, without appealing directly to explicit properties such as expansion. More generally, we construct such a learning algorithm from the assumption that semirandom $k$-XOR has Sum-of-Squares certificates of refutation. This yields the broader implication that any Sum-of-Squares refutation algorithm for semirandom $k$-XOR gives a corresponding algorithm for solving semirandom planted CSPs, and instantiating this reduction with known Sum-of-Squares algorithms for refuting semirandom $k$-XOR gives our main algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reduction from search to refutation for (semi)random CSPs.

papers.title: Counting over Unbreakable Decompositions: A Single-Exponential Parameterized Algorithm for Minimum Bisection
papers.abstract: The Minimum Bisection problem asks whether an $n$-vertex graph can be split into two halves with at most $k$ edges between them. We give a single exponential time algorithm for minimum bisection, running in time $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$. This improves the previous bound of $2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}$ due to Cygan, Komosa, Lokshtanov, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, Saurabh, and Wahlstr\"om (TALG 2021). Our algorithm counts solutions instead of only finding if one exists. We show that our dynamic program can be implemented on top of an unbreakable decomposition using algebraic techniques. Along the way, we compute in time $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$ a tree decomposition with adhesions of size at most $2k$ whose bags are $(3k,k)$-edge-unbreakable inside their own subtrees.

papers.title: All minimum cuts of symmetric submodular functions
papers.abstract: We compute Cunningham's canonical decomposition of a symmetric submodular function on $n$ elements in $O(n^3)$ time. The decomposition represents all minimum cuts in linear space. For the pair $s,t$ produced by Queyranne's algorithm, we construct in $O(n^2)$ time a digraph representing exactly the minimum $st$-cuts of the function. Using this construction in Chekuri and Xu's decomposition algorithm gives the cubic bound.

papers.title: Minimum-Cost $k$-Arborescence Packing in $\tilde O(km+k^4 n)$ Time
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic, strongly polynomial algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(km+k^4n)$ time that finds $k$ arc-disjoint arborescences of minimum total cost in a directed multigraph with $n$ vertices and $m$ arcs. This significantly improves upon the state of the art for $k \ge 2$ with $k=n^{o(1)}$: the prior fastest weakly polynomial and strongly polynomial algorithms take $\tilde{O}(km\sqrt{n}\log C)$ and $\tilde{O}(kmn)$ time (Gabow and Xu, 1989; Gabow, 1995), respectively. Roughly, our technique can be viewed as a way to apply a linear number of \emph{shortest} augmenting paths in near-linear total time for the special case of the weighted matroid intersection problem between the $k$-fold graphic matroid and the indegree partition matroid. This was previously done in the unweighted case by Gabow (1995), but our approach is different. As an extension, we also obtain a deterministic $\tilde{O}(km^{1+o(1)}+k^5n)$-time algorithm for minimum-cost maximum-cardinality packing of $k$ forests in undirected graphs. In particular, this finds $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees of minimum total cost, if they exist. The previous fastest algorithm takes $\tilde{O}(kn^2+m)$ time (Gabow and Westermann, 1992).

papers.title: Connectivity in a New Bounded-Space Dynamic Model
papers.abstract: We introduce a new model for dynamic algorithms in which the algorithm has read-only oracle access to a dynamically changing input and random access to its own bounded workspace. It is a dynamic analogue of the time-space tradeoffs for static inputs studied in complexity theory, where only writable memory counts as space. We study dynamic undirected $s$-$t$ connectivity: after every edge update to an $n$-vertex graph, an algorithm with $S$ words of workspace must report whether $s$ and $t$ are connected. The graph is accessed via adjacency list queries (degree, $j$-th neighbor) or adjacency matrix queries. Our algorithms are randomized; our lower bounds hold for randomized algorithms with $cn$ bits of workspace, $c>0$ a small constant ($cn/\log n$ for the worst-case matrix bound). We prove: (1) With adjacency lists, worst-case time $\tilde\Theta(n^2/S^2)$ per insertion is necessary and sufficient for incremental algorithms. (2) With an adjacency matrix, worst-case time $\tilde\Omega(n^2/S)$ per insertion is necessary for incremental algorithms, and sufficient for $S\ge\sqrt{n}$. (3) With amortization, incremental algorithms achieve $\tilde O(n/S)$ time per insertion with adjacency lists and $\tilde O(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, while $\tilde\Omega(\sqrt{n/S})$ and $\tilde\Omega(n\sqrt{n/S})$, respectively, are necessary. (4) Fully dynamic algorithms need amortized time $\tilde\Omega(n/S)$ per update with adjacency lists and $\tilde\Omega(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, even on forests, where both bounds are tight (lists: under bounded degree). Conventional dynamic connectivity admits polylogarithmic update time with $\Omega(n)$ words of space. In contrast, our lower bounds show that polynomial update time is necessary whenever $S\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$, even for a single pair of vertices and even for incremental algorithms with amortized guarantees.

papers.title: A Near-Optimal Generalized Sorting Algorithm
papers.abstract: We continue the study of the classic \emph{generalized sorting problem}, a basic variant of ordinary sorting. There are $n$ elements and an (initially hidden) total ordering $\pi$ over them. Unlike in ordinary sorting, however, only \emph{some} comparisons are allowed: those given by the edges of an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ on the elements. How many comparisons are needed to find the total ordering? In ordinary sorting, $\Theta(n \log n)$ comparisons are necessary and sufficient. For generalized sorting, however, the best known upper bound has been $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ since the work of Huang, Kannan, and Khanna (FOCS 2011), who even asked whether the problem might in fact require $n^{1+\Omega(1)}$ comparisons. We show that it does not: we give a randomized algorithm that uses $O(n \log^4 n)$ comparisons in expectation. Thus, up to logarithmic factors, generalized sorting is no harder than ordinary sorting.

papers.title: Canonical Cut Hierarchy in Almost-Linear Time via Reduction to Max-Flow
papers.abstract: The canonical cut hierarchy recursively partitions a graph along Tutte-Nash-Williams partitions, choosing the partition with the most number of parts at each step. We give a randomized almost linear-time algorithm for computing this hierarchy in undirected graphs with polynomially bounded capacities via reduction to max-flow. This yields randomized almost linear-time algorithms for computing partition connectivity, strength, both arboricity and fractional arboricity, both integral and fractional spanning tree packing numbers, and implicit representations of the principal partition sequence and a maximum fractional spanning tree packing.

papers.title: Resolving Tusnády's Problem
papers.abstract: We prove a lower bound of $\Omega_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ for the worst-case combinatorial discrepancy of $N$-point sets with respect to anchored boxes in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$. Together with Nikolov's upper bound of the same order and Wei's planar lower bound, this settles Tusn\'ady's problem: the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. The proof combines smoothed product test functions, sampling discretization, and an entropy argument for conditioned Gaussian vectors.

papers.title: Stacking Stars: Minimum-Area Packing with and without Rotation
papers.abstract: We study the problem of packing a given set of polygons into a minimum-area convex container, that is, placing them without overlap so as to minimize the area of their convex hull. Every previously known polynomial-time algorithm with a nontrivial approximation guarantee for packing polygons with arbitrary edge orientations required the polygons to be convex. In fact, an algorithm was not even known when every input polygon was a quadrilateral. We obtain such algorithms for the entire class of star-shaped polygons with unrestricted combinatorial complexity. The stars may be just translated or also rotated. In either case, we give an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm, where $n$ is the number of stars. Likewise, we get $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithms for bin and strip packing, assuming that the diameter of the stars is at most some (small) constant. Previous approximation algorithms for polygon packing focused on convex objects, and the analysis always relied on a density argument, i.e., if the area of the packed objects is at least a fraction $\rho$ of the area of the container, then we have a $(1/\rho)$-approximation. However, star-shaped polygons may need an arbitrarily large area to be packed, even when the total area of the stars approaches $0$ and each star has bounded diameter. This phenomenon prevents the use of density arguments. We instead establish a strong structural property about any packing: Even though the stars can fit together in complicated ways, we can reorganize them into simple stacks, replace these stacks by rectangles, and consider a packing of these rectangles. The rearrangement costs only a factor of $O(\log n)$, which stems from the number of size groups. We complement our algorithms by showing that both the translational and the rotational versions are APX-hard, even for constant complexity stars.

papers.title: Newton Steps are Faster for Linear Complementarity Problems
papers.abstract: Linear Complementarity Problems (LCPs) with sufficient matrices form a well-studied class of problems, dating back from the foundational works of Cottle and Dantzig (1968). LCPs capture convex quadratic programs, and admit reductions from problems such as discounted stochastic games or mean-payoff games. While the original approach for solving these problems was based on pivoting methods, in their 1991 book, Kojima, Megiddo, Noma, and Yoshise introduced an interior point method (IPM) with running time that is polynomial in the input size, but which depends linearly on a certain parameter called the handicap number of the matrix. Despite the ensuing rich literature on sufficient LCP IPMs, the linear dependence on the handicap number has not been improved since then. We present an IPM whose running time depends on the square root of the handicap number. The algorithm can decrease the duality gap by a constant factor in $O\left(\min\left\{\sqrt{n} (1+\kappa),n^{9/8}\sqrt{1+\kappa}\right\}\right)$ iterations. Curiously, this can already be achieved using standard Newton updates. We analyze the IPM in a norm defined by a local weighting, where centralizing Newton steps quadratically converge to the central path, without any dependence on the handicap number. The weights arise from a characterization by Rump (Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 1997, 1998, 2003) of the sign-real spectral radius and its relation to sufficiency; another ingredient of our proof is a new operator norm characterization of the handicap number. Moreover, the connection to Rump's work also enables us to show coNP-completeness of testing sufficiency, and approximation hardness of the handicap number.

papers.title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Dependent Graph Classes
papers.abstract: Monadically dependent graph classes are those in which first-order logic cannot encode all graphs. They include all nowhere dense classes and all classes of bounded twin-width. We show that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically dependent graph class. Together with the known hardness result for hereditary classes that are not monadically dependent, this gives a complete characterization of the hereditary graph classes with fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking. This resolves a central open problem in algorithmic model theory. Our proof combines ideas from structural graph theory (graph decompositions), finite model theory (locality of first-order logic), and model theory (counting types). In particular, we show that in monadically dependent classes, tuples of fixed length have only $|U|^{O(1)}$ types of fixed quantifier rank over any set of parameters $U$.

papers.title: Regret Bounds for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade: Learning the Best Posted-Price Mechanism
papers.abstract: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the perspective of a profit-maximizing broker in a regret minimization framework. At each time step, a new seller and buyer arrive and the broker proposes a trading price to each agent. The trade happens if both agents accept, and the profit of the broker is the difference between the price received from the buyer and the one paid to the seller. At the end of each interaction, the learner only observes whether the trade occurred, and its goal is to achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed pair of prices in hindsight. We start by investigating the adversarial version of the problem, where buyer and seller valuations are generated by an adversary. In this setting, we construct a polynomial-time learning algorithm with a $\tilde O(T^{\frac 23})$ regret rate, which is nearly tight even if the valuations are drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions, thus matching the rate for one-sided pricing. Our adversarial algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction. We then consider valuations drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions satisfying the monotone-hazard-rate (MHR) property and provide a learning algorithm with nearly tight $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is $\tilde \Theta(T^{\frac 35})$. This last result contrasts with the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.

papers.title: Quantum Advantage with Sign-Free Proofs: An Oracle Separation between $\mathsf{StoqMA}$ and $\mathsf{MA}$
papers.abstract: Several landmark oracle results (FOCS 2000, FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) establish strict separations along the chain $\mathsf{MA} \subseteq \mathsf{QCMA} \subseteq \mathsf{QMA}$, showing that quantum verification and quantum witnesses can each provide additional power over classical proof systems. These separations, however, use substantial coherent quantum computation, often through the quantum Fourier transform. We prove that a minimal quantum resource already suffices to outperform every classical verifier. Namely, we show the separation $$\mathsf{MA} \subsetneq \mathsf{StoqMA}$$ relative to a classical oracle. The class $\mathsf{StoqMA}$, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (arXiv 2006), restricts the verifier to classical reversible computation, followed by a single Hadamard-basis measurement. Its power is closely tied to the complexity of stoquastic Hamiltonians, a sign-problem-free and seemingly more tractable class of quantum Hamiltonians. Our separating problem is to determine whether a sparse high-girth graph, given via an adjacency-list oracle, has a large or small Perron--Frobenius eigenvalue. This amounts to a ground-energy estimation task for a related stoquastic Hamiltonian. Our construction builds on a line of work on graph exploration problems with exponential quantum speedups, from welded trees (STOC 2003) to recent constructions (STOC 2021, arXiv 2026).

papers.title: Low-Temperature Sampling via Equilibrium Disagreements
papers.abstract: We develop a new framework for sampling at low temperatures using Glauber dynamics. In this regime, the coexistence of competing modes (commonly referred to as phases) creates bottlenecks that can make worst-case mixing exponentially slow. The main new ingredient in our framework is to relate convergence within a phase to the geometry of disagreements between two independent configurations drawn from that phase. As applications of our approach, we consider three canonical models on random regular graphs that have been central to low-temperature sampling, and establish fast convergence from natural initialisations of Glauber dynamics for every fixed degree. We show: --- For the hard-core model on random bipartite $d$-regular graphs, Glauber dynamics initialised from either one-sided independent set mixes within the corresponding phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps throughout the non-uniqueness regime $\lambda>\lambda_c(d)$. --- For the random-cluster model on random $d$-regular graphs, for every real $q>2$, Glauber dynamics initialised from the all-in edge set mixes within the ordered phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps for all $\beta\geq \beta_c$. Similarly, Glauber dynamics initialised from the all-out edge set mixes within the disordered phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps for $\beta\leq \beta_c$. --- For the ferromagnetic Ising model on random $d$-regular graphs, Glauber dynamics initialised from all-plus or all-minus mixes within the corresponding phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps throughout the low-temperature regime $\beta>\beta_c(d)$. We also give an $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm that combines phase samples into samples from the full distribution, avoiding in particular time-costly approximations of the corresponding partition functions to the target sampling accuracy.

papers.title: Tusnády's problem and online two-sample thinning
papers.abstract: We determine the sharp order of discrepancy in Tusn\'ady's problem in every fixed dimension $d\ge 2$. The largest combinatorial discrepancy of $N$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$, extending Wei's planar result and matching Nikolov's upper bound. More strongly, with high probability, this lower bound holds simultaneously for every subset obtained by deleting at most a sufficiently small fixed fraction of a uniform $N$-point sample. We apply this geometric estimate to online thinning of two independent samples of size $n$ from an unknown common distribution, where observations must be kept or discarded upon arrival. For every fixed dimension $k\ge 1$ and expected deletion budget $\rho n$, with $0<\rho<2$, we prove that the minimax expected prefix discrepancy over lower orthants is $\Theta_{k,\rho}((\log n)^{k+1/2})$. In dimension one, the optimal terminal discrepancy is instead $\Theta_\rho((\log\log n)^{3/2})$, giving a sharp separation between the prefix and terminal objectives. For $k\ge 2$, we obtain terminal bounds differing by a factor of $\log n$. The lower bounds are based on Gaussian small-ball estimates for box-incidence matrices, while the upper bounds use stationary Metropolis thinning and, in one dimension, a terminal cancellation procedure.
